content: A Lewis acid is a chemical species capable of accepting a pair of electrons to form a coordinate covalent bond. The concept of Lewis acids and bases, named after the American chemist Gilbert N. Lewis, is one of several theories used to describe acid-base reactions. The term acid itself can be ambiguous and should always be clarified as either a Lewis acid or a Brønsted-Lowry acid. A Lewis acid is essentially an electrophile or an electron acceptor. Lewis acids typically possess a low-energy Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital (LUMO), which interacts with the Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital (HOMO) of a Lewis base. Unlike Brønsted-Lowry acids, which always donate a hydrogen ion (H+), Lewis acids can be any electrophile, including H+. While all Brønsted-Lowry acids are also Lewis acids, the term Lewis acid is often reserved for those that are not Brønsted-Lowry acids in common usage. The reactivity of Lewis acids can be evaluated using the Hard-Soft Acid-Base (HSAB) concept. However, there is no universally valid measure of Lewis acid strength, as it depends on the specific Lewis base involved. One computational model has predicted Lewis acid strength based on gas-phase fluoride affinity, identifying antimony pentafluoride (SbF5) as having the strongest fluoride affinity among common isolable Lewis acids. Fluoride is considered a hard Lewis base, while softer Lewis bases, such as chloride, are more challenging to study due to computational limitations. Similarly, the study of Lewis acidity in solution is restricted by these same limitations. Common examples of Lewis acids include aluminum chloride (AlCl3), iron(III) chloride (FeCl3), boron trifluoride (BF3), niobium pentachloride (NbCl5), and lanthanide triflates like ytterbium(III) triflate. Many Lewis acids, such as zinc chloride (ZnCl2), are corrosive. Zinc chloride, for instance, is particularly corrosive to cellulose-based materials like paper and cotton, demonstrating how Lewis acidity itself can cause corrosive effects. Since water is a Lewis base, many common Lewis acids react rapidly with water to form hydrates, which are Brønsted acidic. As a result, solutions of many Lewis acids are also Brønsted acidic. For example, when attempting to dry a metal chloride, hydrogen chloride (HCl) and metal oxychlorides are often released as vapors, indicating the formation of a separate chemical compound in the hydrate form. An ate complex is a type of salt formed when a Lewis acid reacts with a base, leading to an increase in the valence of the central atom. In chemical nomenclature, the suffix ate is often added to the name of the central element in such complexes. For instance, the ate complex of a boron compound is referred to as a borate. A specific example is the reaction of trimethylborane with methyllithium, which forms the ate complex Me4B−Li+. This concept was introduced by Georg Wittig in 1958. Similarly, Lewis bases can form onium salts through analogous reactions.
